blocks.text: Common OSCE scenarios include:
Scenario A — History taking
A 28-year-old woman presents with continuous leakage of urine per vaginam following a prolonged labour. Take a focused history and discuss your differential diagnoses.
Scenario B — Examination
Examine a woman with suspected vesicovaginal fistula and describe how you would confirm the diagnosis.
Scenario C — Investigations
A woman presents with continuous urinary incontinence following pelvic surgery. Describe the investigations required to establish the diagnosis and identify the site of the fistula.
Scenario D — Counselling
Explain the diagnosis and management options to a woman diagnosed with an obstetric fistula.
Scenario E — Image interpretation
A dye test demonstrates blue staining of a vaginal swab after dye is instilled into the bladder. Interpret the finding.
A fistula is an abnormal communication between two epithelial-lined surfaces. A genitourinary fistula involves the urinary tract and the genital tract.

items.text: Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF)

blocks.text: Abnormal communication between the urinary bladder and vagina.
Typical presentation: continuous leakage of urine through the vagina, often with otherwise normal voluntary voiding.
2. Ureterovaginal fistula
Abnormal communication between a ureter and the vagina.
Often follows pelvic surgery. The patient may continue to pass urine normally through the urethra while urine leaks vaginally.
3. Urethrovaginal fistula
Abnormal communication between the urethra and vagina.
May cause urinary leakage, often associated with urethral injury, trauma or surgery.
4. Rectovaginal fistula (RVF)
Abnormal communication between the rectum and vagina.
Causes passage of flatus or faeces through the vagina. Strictly speaking, this is a genital fistula rather than a urinary fistula.
Other relevant fistulas include vesicouterine fistula (bladder to uterus), ureterouterine fistula and complex fistulas involving multiple pelvic structures.

rows: Prolonged obstructed labour, pressure necrosis, direct birth trauma
Pelvic fracture, penetrating injury, sexual trauma
Cervical, bladder or other pelvic cancers
Selected cases involving destructive inflammatory disease or infection

blocks.text: Important distinction: In many low-resource settings, obstetric fistula is strongly associated with prolonged obstructed labour. In high-resource surgical settings, a significant proportion of vesicovaginal fistulas are related to pelvic surgery.
Understanding the mechanism helps you explain the history and predict the findings.
During prolonged obstructed labour, the fetal presenting part may compress the bladder, urethra or adjacent tissues against the maternal pelvis.
Prolonged obstructed labour
Prolonged compression of pelvic soft tissues
Ischaemia and tissue necrosis
Tissue breakdown and fistula formation
Continuous urinary leakage through the vagina
The fistula may become apparent several days after delivery as necrotic tissue separates.
Pelvic surgery may cause direct injury, inadvertent suturing, devascularisation or delayed tissue breakdown involving the bladder or ureter.

items.text: Persistent wetness and urine-associated skin irritation.
Vulval excoriation and dermatitis.
Recurrent urinary tract infections.
Vaginal stenosis or scarring in some cases.
Social isolation, stigma, depression and relationship difficulties.
Renal impairment, particularly if ureteric obstruction or upper urinary tract damage is present.

blocks.text: In the OSCE, approach the patient respectfully. Fistula can be associated with profound embarrassment and social exclusion.

items.text: Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Confirm the patient's identity.
Explain that you would like to ask about her symptoms and medical or obstetric history.
Obtain consent and ensure privacy.
Offer a chaperone when appropriate, particularly if an intimate examination may follow.
Reassure her that the discussion is confidential and non-judgmental.

blocks.text: Example opening:

"I'm sorry that you've been experiencing this problem. I understand that leakage can be distressing. I'd like to ask some questions to understand when it started, what the leakage is like and how it is affecting you. Is that okay?"
Establish exactly what is leaking.

items.text: Is it urine, faeces, flatus, vaginal discharge or a combination?
When did it begin?
Is the leakage continuous or intermittent?
Does it occur during coughing, sneezing, exercise or urgency?
Can she pass urine normally through the urethra?
Does the leakage worsen when standing, walking or sleeping?
Is there a noticeable smell or blood in the fluid?

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Continuous leakage following prolonged labour or pelvic surgery strongly suggests a urinary fistula, particularly VVF. Leakage with coughing or exertion alone suggests stress urinary incontinence, although the two conditions can coexist.
This is especially important when obstetric fistula is suspected.

items.text: Gravidity and parity.
Date and outcome of the most recent pregnancy.
Duration of labour and whether it was obstructed.
Place of delivery and whether skilled assistance was available.
Mode of delivery: vaginal, instrumental or caesarean section.
Stillbirth or neonatal death.
Perineal tears, episiotomy or other birth injuries.
Whether leakage began immediately after delivery or several days later.
Previous fistula repair or pelvic surgery.
Previous hysterectomy, caesarean section or pelvic surgery.
Previous pelvic radiotherapy.
Cervical or other pelvic malignancy.
Pelvic trauma.
Previous urinary tract infections or urinary tract abnormalities.
Prior operations for incontinence or prolapse.

rows: Upper urinary tract obstruction, infection or injury
Urinary tract injury, stones or malignancy
Trauma, malignancy or another pelvic disorder
Passage of flatus or faeces per vagina
Dehydration, renal impairment or urinary obstruction
Weight loss or persistent pelvic pain

blocks.text: This is frequently overlooked in examinations.

items.text: Effect on work, schooling and daily activities.
Access to clean water, sanitary materials and laundry.
Relationship difficulties or fear of abandonment.
Social exclusion and stigma.
Emotional distress, hopelessness or depression.
Availability of family support and access to specialist treatment.

blocks.text: Ask permission before discussing sexual function or relationship concerns. Do not assume that the patient is sexually active or married.

blocks.title: Urgent assessment is required if the patient has:

items.text: Fever with systemic illness or suspected sepsis.
Flank pain with suspected ureteric obstruction.
Oliguria, anuria or acute kidney injury.
Heavy bleeding or severe pelvic pain.
A suspected malignant fistula.
Recent pelvic surgery with suspected urinary tract injury.

blocks.text: In an OSCE, you should explain the examination, obtain consent and demonstrate a structured approach. Intimate examination must be performed by a suitably trained clinician with appropriate privacy and a chaperone.

items.text: General appearance and nutritional status.
Temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate.
Hydration.
Pallor, if anaemia is suspected.
Signs of systemic infection.
Skin irritation, excoriation or ulceration from persistent urine exposure.
Mobility and functional impact.
Surgical scars.
Suprapubic tenderness or a palpable distended bladder.
Pelvic or abdominal masses.
Renal angle tenderness.
Signs of peritonism, if there is concern about an acute complication.

blocks.text: A palpable bladder does not exclude a fistula. Normal bladder emptying also does not exclude a ureterovaginal fistula.

blocks.title: With consent and a chaperone, inspect for:

items.text: Persistent wetness.
Vulval dermatitis and excoriation.
Maceration or ulceration.
Scarring or tissue loss.
Evidence of previous surgery.
Visible urine leakage from the vagina.
Faecal contamination if a rectovaginal fistula is suspected.

blocks.text: A trained examiner may use a vaginal speculum to inspect the vaginal walls and identify:

items.text: The site and approximate size of a fistulous opening.
Leakage of urine through an opening.
Tissue necrosis or inflammation.
Scarring or vaginal stenosis.
Suspicious lesions suggestive of malignancy.

blocks.text: A small fistula may be difficult to visualise. A normal initial speculum examination does not exclude the diagnosis.

blocks.title: Depending on the presentation, the clinician may perform:

items.text: Bimanual pelvic examination for masses or tenderness.
Rectal examination if rectovaginal involvement is suspected.
Neurological assessment if neurogenic bladder dysfunction is a possibility.

blocks.text: Do not perform painful or unnecessary examinations simply to complete an OSCE checklist.
The choice depends on the suspected site, cause and complexity of the fistula.
This is a classic OSCE investigation for differentiating a bladder fistula from a ureterovaginal fistula.
Principle: Dye instilled into the bladder stains swabs if urine is leaking directly from the bladder into the vagina.
The test is performed by a trained clinician using appropriate sterile technique and a suitable dye, commonly dilute methylene blue.

items.text: Blue staining of a vaginal swab supports a bladder-to-vagina communication.
Wet swabs without blue staining raise suspicion of urine arriving from a source not exposed to the bladder dye, such as a ureterovaginal fistula.
Results can be inconclusive, and mixed fistulas or technical problems may complicate interpretation.

blocks.text: The exact swab arrangement and interpretation depend on the local protocol. A dye test should not replace further assessment when the diagnosis remains uncertain.

blocks.title: Allows direct visualisation of the bladder and may help identify:

items.text: The fistulous opening.
Its relationship to the ureteric orifices.
Bladder inflammation or other pathology.
Associated foreign material or surgical injury.
CT urography: useful when ureteric injury, obstruction or urinary tract anatomy needs clarification.
CT cystography: can help demonstrate a bladder leak when appropriately indicated.
MRI pelvis: useful for selected complex fistulas, surrounding soft-tissue anatomy or suspected malignancy.
Ultrasound of the kidneys and urinary tract: assesses hydronephrosis and other upper urinary tract abnormalities.
Retrograde pyelography: may be used to define a suspected ureteric injury or fistula.
Urinalysis.
Urine culture and sensitivity if infection is suspected.
Serum creatinine and electrolytes.
Full blood count when anaemia or infection is suspected.
Additional investigations directed by possible malignancy or associated conditions.

blocks.text: A biopsy may be needed if a malignant lesion is suspected.
The most important differentials are other causes of urinary leakage.

rows: Continuous vaginal urine leakage; bladder dye may stain vaginal swabs
Vaginal urine leakage despite continued urethral voiding; bladder dye may not stain the leaking fluid
Leakage with coughing, sneezing, lifting or exertion
Leakage associated with incomplete bladder emptying or retention
Usually not urine; investigate infection or other causes
May cause lifelong or longstanding continuous leakage, particularly in a young patient
Passage of flatus or faeces through the vagina

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Continuous leakage is a key clue, but it is not sufficient by itself to distinguish every urinary fistula. The history, examination and appropriate investigations must be considered together.
Management depends on the fistula's cause, size, site, tissue condition, duration and associated urinary tract injury.

items.text: Assess for sepsis, urinary obstruction, renal impairment and other urgent complications.
Treat confirmed urinary infection according to culture results and local guidance.
Protect the vulval and perineal skin with gentle cleansing, careful drying and appropriate barrier preparations.
Assess renal function and the upper urinary tract where indicated.
Refer to an experienced fistula surgeon or appropriate urogynaecology/urology service.
Provide counselling, emotional support and practical assistance.

blocks.text: Antibiotics should not be prescribed automatically for every fistula in the absence of an indication.
Selected small, recent fistulas may close with continuous bladder drainage using a catheter, particularly when recognised early after surgery and when tissue damage is limited.
This requires specialist assessment and follow-up. Conservative treatment is less likely to succeed in established obstetric fistulas caused by extensive tissue necrosis.
Surgical repair is the definitive treatment for many established fistulas.

items.text: Adequate exposure and identification of the fistula.
Excision of non-viable tissue when appropriate.
Tension-free, watertight closure.
Preservation of ureteric orifices and surrounding structures.
Interposition of vascularised tissue in selected complex or recurrent cases.
Appropriate postoperative bladder drainage and follow-up.

blocks.text: The timing of repair is individualised. Active infection, inflammation, tissue condition, nutritional status and the mechanism of injury influence when surgery should be performed.
For ureterovaginal fistula, treatment may require ureteric stenting or reconstructive surgery, depending on the location and severity of the injury.

items.text: Maintain the prescribed bladder drainage.
Monitor urine output, pain, temperature and signs of infection.
Follow the surgeon's catheter-removal and imaging protocol.
Assess for persistent leakage or recurrence.
Provide skin care and psychological support.
Discuss sexual health and return to normal activities when clinically appropriate.

blocks.text: Successful treatment extends beyond closing the fistula.

items.text: Counselling and peer support.
Treatment of depression or other psychological difficulties.
Pelvic floor rehabilitation when indicated.
Sexual health counselling after recovery.
Social reintegration and support with education or employment.
Family planning and advice regarding future pregnancies.

blocks.text: Women with previous obstetric fistula need individualised counselling about future pregnancy and delivery planning, ideally through a specialist obstetric service.

"This is a woman presenting with continuous urinary leakage per vaginam following prolonged obstructed labour. Examination demonstrates persistent vulvovaginal wetness and a fistulous opening on speculum examination. A bladder dye test demonstrates blue staining of the vaginal swab, supporting a diagnosis of vesicovaginal fistula. I would assess renal function, exclude urinary infection and upper urinary tract injury, and arrange specialist fistula assessment."

"This patient has continuous urinary leakage per vaginam following pelvic surgery but retains the ability to void urine through the urethra. The bladder dye test does not demonstrate blue staining of the vaginal swabs. A ureterovaginal fistula is suspected. I would arrange appropriate urinary tract imaging, assess renal function and refer urgently to urology or a specialist fistula team."

"The patient reports passage of flatus and faecal material through the vagina. This raises suspicion of a rectovaginal fistula. I would establish the history of obstetric trauma, surgery, inflammatory disease and malignancy, followed by a consented examination and appropriate specialist investigations."
These reports are deliberately concise: present the key symptoms, relevant positive findings, likely diagnosis and next step.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the most common symptom of vesicovaginal fistula?
Continuous leakage of urine through the vagina, often beginning after obstructed labour or pelvic surgery.
Q2. What is the difference between VVF and ureterovaginal fistula?

VVF connects the bladder to the vagina. Ureterovaginal fistula connects a ureter to the vagina. In both, the patient may have continuous leakage, but normal urethral voiding can persist in ureterovaginal fistula.
Q3. Why does obstetric fistula occur after prolonged labour?
Sustained compression of pelvic tissues can cause ischaemia and necrosis, followed by tissue breakdown and formation of an abnormal communication.
Q4. What is the purpose of a bladder dye test?
It helps determine whether leaking fluid communicates directly with the bladder. Blue staining of vaginal swabs after bladder dye instillation supports a bladder-origin fistula.
Q5. Can a ureterovaginal fistula occur when a woman passes urine normally?

Yes. Urine can still flow from the unaffected kidney or through the unaffected portion of the urinary tract into the bladder, allowing normal urethral voiding while urine from an injured ureter leaks into the vagina.
Q6. Is surgery always immediately required?

No. Selected recent, small fistulas may close with continuous bladder drainage. Established fistulas often require reconstructive surgery, and timing depends on the tissue condition and associated injuries.
Q7. What complications should you look for?
Skin excoriation, recurrent urinary infection, scarring, psychological distress, social isolation and renal impairment when the upper urinary tract is affected.
Q8. What is the role of cystoscopy?
It allows direct assessment of the bladder, helps locate the fistulous opening and clarifies its relationship to the ureteric orifices.
Q9. What is the difference between a fistula and stress urinary incontinence?

A fistula is an abnormal anatomical communication causing leakage through the genital tract. Stress urinary incontinence is leakage through the urethra associated with increased intra-abdominal pressure.
Q10. What is the most important non-surgical aspect of management?
Comprehensive supportive care, including skin protection, infection assessment, psychological support, counselling and social reintegration.

items.text: Failing to ask whether leakage is continuous or associated with coughing or urgency.
Forgetting to establish the relationship between symptoms and childbirth or pelvic surgery.
Assuming all vaginal fluid leakage is urinary.
Confusing VVF with ureterovaginal fistula.
Performing an intimate examination without explaining it, obtaining consent or offering a chaperone.
Claiming a negative dye test excludes every type of fistula.
Ignoring renal function and possible ureteric obstruction.
Prescribing antibiotics without assessing whether infection is present.
Discussing surgical repair without addressing psychological distress and social isolation.

A — Assess complications and associated injuries.

content_groups.group_title: Five things to remember in the exam

items.text: Continuous urinary leakage after obstructed labour strongly suggests obstetric VVF.
Continuous leakage after pelvic surgery raises concern for bladder or ureteric injury.
Normal urethral voiding does not exclude a urinary fistula.
Dye testing, cystoscopy and appropriate imaging help establish the diagnosis.
Management includes specialist treatment, skin care, psychosocial support and long-term follow-up.

A 26-year-old woman presents with continuous leakage of urine per vaginam 10 days after a prolonged obstructed labour. She can still pass some urine through the urethra. A bladder dye test causes blue staining of a vaginal swab.
What is the most likely diagnosis?

Vesicovaginal fistula
